title: Unified Theory of Relaxation in Equilibrium and Nonequilibrium Glass-Forming Liquids
authors: Zi-Long Wang, Qi-Lu Yuan, Yun-Jiang Wang, Jack F. Douglas, Matteo Baggioli, Zhao-Yan Sun, Wen-Sheng Xu
abstract: Understanding how structural relaxation evolves from equilibrium to nonequilibrium conditions remains a central problem in glass physics. Using simulations of model glass formers under steady shear, we show that external driving progressively suppresses the stringlike cooperative rearrangements that control relaxation in equilibrium, leading to dramatically faster dynamics. A theory based on collective motion and a shear-dependent effective temperature independently determined from fluctuation-dissipation relations quantitatively predicts the structural relaxation time across the full range of temperatures and shear rates investigated without additional nonequilibrium fitting parameters. These results show that equilibrium and nonequilibrium relaxation are governed by the same underlying cooperative mechanism, but they occur under different effective thermodynamic conditions under steady shear. More broadly, our study provides a unified microscopic description of thermal and mechanically driven dynamics in glass-forming liquids.
summary: This work addresses how structural relaxation behaves when driven by shear stress versus thermal fluctuations. The authors propose a unified theory showing that both regimes are governed by the same cooperative mechanism, quantified by introducing an effective temperature derived from fluctuation-dissipation relations. This provides a powerful tool for describing non-equilibrium dynamics in disordered materials.
main_problem: The central problem is unifying the description of structural relaxation dynamics in glass-forming liquids across both equilibrium (thermal) and non-equilibrium (mechanically driven) conditions.
main_result: The study shows that external driving accelerates relaxation by suppressing cooperative stringlike rearrangements, leading to a unified theory based on an effective temperature derived from fluctuation-dissipation relations.
method: The authors developed a microscopic theory extending the String Model by incorporating a shear-dependent effective temperature ($T_{	ext{map}}$) determined independently via generalized Fluctuation-Dissipation Relations (FDR).
model_or_system: The research uses simulations of model glass formers, such as the KABLJ binary Lennard-Jones system and polymer melts, to study structural relaxation.
key_observables: Structural relaxation time ($	au_\alpha$), self-intermediate scattering function ($F_s(q, t)$), characteristic string length ($L$), and various definitions of effective temperature ($T_{	ext{map}}$, $T_{	ext{avg}}$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), shear rate ($\dot{\gamma}$), and the structural relaxation time scale ($	au_0$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics share a single underlying cooperative mechanism, which can be parameterized by an effective thermodynamic condition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $F_s(q, t)$ decay accelerating with shear rate; they also show the suppression of cooperative strings under shear and compare different methods for determining the effective temperature ($T_{	ext{map}}$ vs. $T_{	ext{avg}}$) across various systems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the problem (unifying dynamics) to developing a theoretical framework based on collective motion and an effective temperature derived from FDRs, culminating in quantitative predictions that successfully map non-equilibrium data onto equilibrium forms.
why_interesting: While focused on classical glass physics, the rigorous application of generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorems to define an 'effective' thermodynamic state under external driving mirrors techniques used in analyzing open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
